fragments.title: Note #1 — When a lie costs a life
fragments.body: In 2018, false rumours spread on Facebook in Sri Lanka blaming Muslims for poisoning food. Within days, mobs attacked Muslim-owned shops and mosques. At least two people were killed. The Sri Lankan government temporarily blocked social media to stop the violence. Facebook later acknowledged it had failed to act on warnings about the content. The rumour was fabricated. The deaths were real.

fragments.title: Note #2 — The photo that wasn't
fragments.body: In 2015, a photo of a drowned toddler on a Turkish beach became one of the most shared images of the refugee crisis. Days later, a different photo circulated claiming to show the same child. It was actually a photo of a different boy, alive and safe. The fake was shared millions of times by people who meant well. The real family had to publicly deny their son was dead.

fragments.title: Note #3 — The name that ruined lives
fragments.body: After the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, users on Reddit and 4chan tried to identify the attacker by scanning photos. They named the wrong person — a missing college student who had died by suicide months earlier. His family, still grieving, was harassed online. His name was cleared days later, but the damage stuck. Crowdsourced detective work without verification is not fact-checking.

fragments.title: Note #4 — A village destroyed by a message
fragments.body: In 2018, false messages on WhatsApp in India claimed children were being kidnapped by strangers. Mobs formed. At least two dozen people were killed across several states by crowds who believed they were stopping abductions. WhatsApp later limited message forwarding and added a "forwarded" label. The messages were not true. The mobs were not heroes.

fragments.title: Note #5 — The deepfake that moved money
fragments.body: In February 2024, a finance worker in Hong Kong joined a video call with what appeared to be the company's CFO and several colleagues. They were all deepfakes. He transferred HK$200 million — about US$25 million — to fraudsters, believing the order was real. It was one of the largest deepfake frauds on record. The meeting looked normal. Nothing about it was.

fragments.title: Note #6 — The map that moved a hurricane
fragments.body: In 2019, a national weather agency issued a projection showing a hurricane's path. A government official shared an altered version, drawn with a marker, extending the danger zone to cover an area it had never been forecast to reach. The agency publicly corrected it. The map was false. But for days, millions of people were told the storm was coming for them.

fragments.title: Note #7 — Why this is in a game
fragments.body: None of the incidents in these notes were solved by a clever algorithm. Every one of them was eventually corrected — by a journalist, a relative, an official, or a stranger who checked before sharing. That is the whole skill: checking before you share. Every person who paused to verify is the reason the next rumour died faster than it spread.

fragments.title: Note #8 — How to check
fragments.body: Before you share something that makes you angry, scared, or certain — stop. Search the claim. Look for the original source. Check whether the same image appears somewhere older or from a different country. Ask who benefits if you believe it. Fact-checking is not a talent.
